questions.question: Among the elements B, Al, Ga, In and Tl, the number of elements that possess completely filled $d$-orbitals but do not have any $f$-electrons in their ground state electronic configuration is ____.
questions.solution:
The ground state electronic configurations of the given Group 13 elements are:

B ($Z = 5$): [He] $2s^{2} 2p^{1}$
Al ($Z = 13$): [Ne] $3s^{2} 3p^{1}$
Ga ($Z = 31$): [Ar] $3d^{10} 4s^{2} 4p^{1}$
In ($Z = 49$): [Kr] $4d^{10} 5s^{2} 5p^{1}$
Tl ($Z = 81$): [Xe] $4f^{14} 5d^{10} 6s^{2} 6p^{1}$

From the electronic configurations, B and Al do not have any d-electrons.

Ga and In possess completely filled d-orbitals ($3d^{10}$ and $4d^{10}$ respectively) and do not have any f-electrons.

Tl possesses completely filled d-orbitals ($5d^{10}$) but also contains completely filled f-orbitals ($4f^{14}$).

Thus, only Ga and In satisfy the given conditions. The number of such elements is $2$.

Answer: $2$

options: the inert pair effect tightly holding the valence $6p$ electron in thallium.
strong shielding of the increased nuclear charge by the intervening $4f$ and $5d$ electrons in thallium.
the higher electronegativity of indium as compared to thallium.
poor shielding of the increased nuclear charge by the intervening $4f$ and $5d$ electrons in thallium.
questions.solution:
In moving from indium to thallium in Group 13, the atomic number increases by $32$. This involves the filling of $4f$ and $5d$ orbitals before the $6s$ and $6p$ orbitals are filled.

The $4f$ and $5d$ electrons have a highly diffused shape and provide poor shielding for the valence electrons against the increased nuclear charge.

Due to this poor shielding, the effective nuclear charge experienced by the valence electrons in thallium is significantly higher. This pulls the valence electrons closer to the nucleus, causing the atomic radius of thallium to be only marginally larger than that of indium.

The higher effective nuclear charge also holds the valence electrons more tightly, which results in an unexpectedly higher first ionisation enthalpy for thallium compared to indium.

Answer: poor shielding of the increased nuclear charge by the intervening $4f$ and $5d$ electrons in thallium.

$\text{BCl}$
$\text{TlCl}$

questions.solution:
The elements of Group 13 exhibit $+3$ and $+1$ oxidation states.

As we move down the group from Boron to Thallium, the stability of the $+1$ oxidation state increases while the stability of the $+3$ oxidation state decreases. This is due to the inert pair effect, which is the reluctance of the $ns^2$ electrons to participate in bonding because of the poor shielding effect of intervening $d$ and $f$ orbitals in heavier elements.

Therefore, for Thallium (Tl), the $+1$ oxidation state is thermodynamically more stable than the $+3$ oxidation state. Consequently, $\text{TlCl}$ is the most stable monohalide among the given options, whereas B, Al, and Ga predominantly form trihalides (like $\text{BCl}_3$, $\text{AlCl}_3$, and $\text{GaCl}_3$).

Answer: $\text{TlCl}$

Statement (C) is correct. The stability of the $+3$ oxidation state decreases down the group. Consequently, the tendency of the $+3$ ions to accept two electrons and get reduced to the $+1$ state increases. Thus, the oxidising character of the $+3$ state increases in the order $\text{Al}^{3+} < \text{Ga}^{3+} < \text{In}^{3+} < \text{Tl}^{3+}$.

Statement (D) is correct. For gallium and indium, the $+3$ oxidation state is more stable than the $+1$ oxidation state. It is only for thallium that the $+1$ state becomes more stable than the $+3$ state.

Statement (E) is incorrect. $\text{Tl}^+$ is highly stable in aqueous solution and does not disproportionate. Instead, it is $\text{Ga}^+$ and $\text{In}^+$ that undergo disproportionation in aqueous solutions to form the respective metal and $+3$ ions.

Therefore, the correct statements are (B), (C), and (D).

options: $\text{BI}_3$ is the strongest Lewis acid because the size mismatch between the $2p$ orbital of boron and the $5p$ orbital of iodine makes $p\pi-p\pi$ back-bonding least effective.

questions.solution:
The Lewis acid strength of boron trihalides follows the order $\text{BF}_3 < \text{BCl}_3 < \text{BBr}_3 < \text{BI}_3$.

This trend is explained by $p\pi-p\pi$ back-bonding. In $\text{BF}_3$, the filled $2p$ orbital of fluorine overlaps effectively with the empty $2p$ orbital of boron due to their similar sizes. This back-donation of electrons partially satisfies the electron deficiency of the boron atom, making $\text{BF}_3$ a weaker Lewis acid.

As the size of the halogen atom increases from fluorine to iodine, the energy and size of its valence $p$ orbitals increase ($3p$ for $\text{Cl}$, $4p$ for $\text{Br}$, $5p$ for $\text{I}$). The overlap between the $2p$ orbital of boron and the larger $p$ orbitals of the heavier halogens becomes progressively less effective due to the size mismatch.

Consequently, the extent of back-bonding is minimum in $\text{BI}_3$, leaving the boron atom highly electron-deficient. Thus, $\text{BI}_3$ acts as the strongest Lewis acid among the boron trihalides.

Answer: $\text{BI}_3$ is the strongest Lewis acid because the size mismatch between the $2p$ orbital of boron and the $5p$ orbital of iodine makes $p\pi-p\pi$ back-bonding least effective.
